newsitem.title: JAPAN: DKB says regrets prosecutors' raid of its offices.
newsitem.headline: DKB says regrets prosecutors' raid of its offices.

text.p: Major Japanese bank Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd (DKB) said on Tuesday that it regrets the raid of its headquarters by Tokyo prosecutors.
A bank spokesman said that prosecutors started searching its headquarters in Tokyo from 9 a.m. (0000 GMT).
"We find it extremely regrettable that we have brought on ourselves a situation in which Tokyo prosecutors have searched (our offices). We will cooperate fully with investigations," he said.
He said, however, that the bank's public relations office did not yet know the reason for the prosecutors' actions.
He also declined comment on media reports that the bank provided questionable loans to a racketeer at the centre of the Nomura Securities Co Ltd scandal.

The spokesman also declined to comment on a report in Tuesday's Yomiuri Shimbun daily which said that the bank had provided questionable loans worth some 600 million yen without collateral to a "sokaiya" racketeer, Ryuichi Koike, a principal figure in the Nomura scandal.
The Yomiuri said that the loans were extended in the autumn of 1994 to help Koike repay interest on his huge borrowings from DKB, which had become non-performing.
Prosecutors are particularly focussing on whether the loans violated the Commercial Code or involved breach of trust, the newspaper said.
Some financial analysts have said that if DKB extended loans to the sokaiya without any collateral and was well aware that the loans would not be paid back, legal action could be brought against it.
Koike and his younger brother Yoshinori Koike were arrested last Thursday on suspicion of violating Japan's Commercial Code by taking some 50 million yen in illegal payments from Nomura.
Two former Nomura executives and a third senior Nomura official have also been arrested in the case.
After the Nomura payoff scandal was revealed in early March, media reports said DKB loaned three billion yen in 1989 to a real estate company owned by the younger Koike.
DKB has repeatedly said it cannot comment on transactions with individuals.
The elder Koike reportedly used the money to buy 300,000 shares in each of the nation's top four brokerages, including Nomura, and put up the shares as collateral for DKB loans.

Media reports have also said that DKB and a financial firm which has a close relationship with DKB, Daiwa Shinyo, provided another three billion yen to Koike in 1990 for a golf course development project.
Separately, DKB guaranteed loans worth about two billion yen provided by Daiwa Shinyo to Koike from 1992, the reports said.

Jiji news agency reported on Tuesday that prosecutors also searched Daiwa Shinyo's office in Tokyo on Tuesday morning, but an official at the firm said he had no information on any such development. Jiji also said that overall loans provided to Koike from DKB and Daiwa Shinyo, a non-bank financial institution, totalled about 30 billion yen.
The Daiwa Shinyo official said he did not know about any questionable loans to Koike.
